Gallium
Paul-Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran
France
From Gallia, the Latin name of France.
Mendeleev had predicted it as «eka-aluminium». Lecoq discovered it in 1875 with a spectroscope, and Mendeleev wrote to him that the measured density was wrong: he was right.
It is obtained as a by-product of processing bauxite and zinc, mostly in China.
LEDs, lasers in Blu-ray players, 5G phone chips, solar panels for satellites.
It melts at 30 °C: if you hold a piece in your hand it melts like chocolate!
Germanium
Clemens Winkler
Germany
From Germania, the Latin name of Germany.
It was the «eka-silicon» predicted by Mendeleev. Winkler found it in 1886 in the mineral argyrodite, and its properties matched the prediction almost perfectly.
It is obtained from zinc-processing residues and coal ash.
Optical fibres, infrared night-vision lenses, space solar cells; the first transistors were made of germanium.
The first transistor in history (1947) was made of germanium, not silicon.
Arsenic
Albertus Magnus
Germany
From the Greek arsenikon, «yellow», the name of the mineral orpiment.
Its minerals were known to the ancients. Albertus Magnus is credited with first isolating it around 1250.
It occurs in minerals such as arsenopyrite and realgar; it is obtained as a by-product of copper and gold smelting.
Semiconductors (gallium arsenide), wood preservatives (now restricted), alloys for lead-acid batteries.
For centuries it was the «poison of kings». Today one of its compounds is used as a medicine against a form of leukaemia.
Selenium
Jöns Jacob Berzelius
Sweden
From the Greek selene, «Moon», because it resembles tellurium (from the Latin tellus, «Earth»).
Berzelius found it in 1817 in the sludge of a sulfuric-acid factory.
It is obtained from the sludge left by copper refining.
Old photocopiers, glass (to remove green tints or to colour it red), supplements, solar cells.
It conducts electricity better when it is lit: it was used in the first experiments to send pictures over a distance.
Bromine
Antoine-Jérôme Balard; Carl Löwig
France / Germany
From the Greek bromos, «stench».
Balard, a 23-year-old student, discovered it in 1826 in the brine of the salt marshes of Montpellier. Löwig had isolated it shortly before but published later.
It is extracted from Dead Sea water and from underground brines.
Flame retardants, water treatment, medicines, film photography (silver bromide).
It is one of only two elements that are liquid at room temperature (the other is mercury).
Krypton
William Ramsay, Morris Travers
England
From the Greek kryptos, «hidden».
It was found in 1898 in the residue left after evaporating liquid air, a few weeks before neon.
Present in air in traces (about 1 part per million).
Photographic flash lamps, high-efficiency light bulbs, insulating windows, lasers.
From 1960 to 1983 the metre was defined using the light emitted by krypton-86. And Superman's kryptonite was named after it!
Rubidium
Robert Bunsen, Gustav Kirchhoff
Germany
From the Latin rubidus, «deep red», for the red lines in its spectrum.
It was discovered in 1861 with the spectroscope just invented by Bunsen and Kirchhoff, while analysing the mineral lepidolite.
It is obtained as a by-product of lithium, from the minerals lepidolite and pollucite.
Atomic clocks, research on Bose-Einstein condensates, purple fireworks.
The rubidium atomic clocks in GPS satellites help your phone know where you are.
Strontium
Adair Crawford
Scotland
From the village of Strontian, in Scotland, where the mineral was found.
Crawford recognised a new mineral in 1790 in the lead mines of Strontian. Davy isolated the metal in 1808.
It is extracted from celestine and strontianite (China, Spain, Mexico).
Red fireworks and signal flares, ferrite magnets, toothpaste for sensitive teeth.
The bright red of fireworks almost always comes from strontium.
Yttrium
Johan Gadolin
Finland
From the Swedish village of Ytterby, whose quarry gave its name to four elements.
Gadolin discovered it in 1794 in a black mineral found in the Ytterby quarry, near Stockholm.
It occurs in monazite sands and in clays of southern China, together with the rare earths.
White LEDs, YAG lasers, superconductors, zirconia dental crowns, old colour TV screens (the red).
Ytterby is a tiny village, but it gave its name to yttrium, ytterbium, terbium and erbium!
Zirconium
Martin Heinrich Klaproth
Germany
From the Persian zargun, «gold-coloured», the name of the gem zircon.
Klaproth discovered it in 1789 while analysing a zircon from Sri Lanka. The metal was isolated by Berzelius in 1824.
It is extracted from zircon sands in Australia and South Africa.
Fuel cladding in nuclear reactors, dental ceramics, ceramic knives, fake diamonds (cubic zirconia).
Zircons are among the oldest minerals on Earth: some Australian crystals are 4.4 billion years old.
Niobium
Charles Hatchett
England
From Niobe, daughter of Tantalus in Greek mythology, because it always comes with tantalum.
Hatchett found it in 1801 in an American mineral and called it columbium. In 1844 Heinrich Rose clearly distinguished it from tantalum and called it niobium.
Brazil produces about 90% of the world's niobium.
High-strength steels for bridges and pipelines, superconducting magnets in MRI scanners and at CERN, coloured anodised jewellery.
The superconducting magnets of CERN's LHC use kilometres of niobium-titanium cable.
Molybdenum
Carl Wilhelm Scheele
Sweden
From the Greek molybdos, «lead», because its ores were confused with lead ores.
In 1778 Scheele realised that molybdenite was neither graphite nor lead. The metal was isolated by Peter Jacob Hjelm in 1781.
It is extracted from molybdenite (China, Chile, United States).
Very strong steels, catalysts, lubricants, filaments; it is essential for enzymes in plants and animals.
In the First World War it was used to strengthen tank armour.
Technetium
Emilio Segrè, Carlo Perrier
Italy
From the Greek technetos, «artificial»: it was the first element produced artificially.
Segrè and Perrier found it in Palermo in 1937 in a molybdenum foil that had been bombarded in the Berkeley cyclotron.
In nature there are only minute traces in uranium ores; it is produced in nuclear reactors. It has also been seen in red giant stars.
Technetium-99m is the most widely used radioisotope in nuclear medicine: tens of millions of scans every year.
It was discovered in Italy! And it is the lightest element with no stable isotope at all.
Ruthenium
Karl Ernst Claus
Russia
From Ruthenia, the Latin name of Russia.
Claus isolated it in 1844 at the University of Kazan from the residues of refining platinum from the Urals.
It is obtained together with platinum, mainly in South Africa and Russia.
Electrical contacts, hard disks, fountain-pen nibs, catalysts, experimental solar cells.
It is one of the platinum-group metals, among the rarest in the Earth's crust.
Rhodium
William Hyde Wollaston
England
From the Greek rhodon, «rose», for the colour of its salts.
Wollaston discovered it in 1803 while processing raw platinum, shortly after finding palladium.
It is obtained together with platinum, mostly in South Africa.
Catalytic converters, jewellery plating (white gold), mirrors, thermocouples.
It is often the most expensive metal in the world: in some years it has cost over 20,000 euros per ounce.
Palladium
William Hyde Wollaston
England
From the asteroid Pallas, discovered the year before.
Wollaston discovered it in 1803 and at first sold it anonymously in a London shop.
It is mined in Russia and South Africa, together with nickel and platinum.
Catalytic converters, electronics, dentistry, white gold, hydrogen purification.
Palladium can absorb up to 900 times its own volume of hydrogen, like a sponge.
Silver
Known since antiquity
From the Old English seolfor; the symbol Ag comes from the Latin argentum, which also gave Argentina its name.
It has been used for jewellery and coins for over 5,000 years. It was sometimes found pure in nature.
It is mined in Mexico, Peru and China, often together with lead, zinc and copper.
Jewellery, cutlery, solar panels, electronics, mirrors, disinfectants, photography.
It is the best conductor of electricity and heat of all metals.
Cadmium
Friedrich Stromeyer
Germany
From cadmia, the ancient Latin name of zinc carbonate.
Stromeyer discovered it in 1817 while investigating why a zinc oxide changed colour.
It is obtained as a by-product of zinc.
Nickel-cadmium batteries (now restricted), yellow and red pigments for painters, solar cells, nuclear control rods.
Monet's bright yellows and reds were cadmium pigments.
Indium
Ferdinand Reich, Theodor Richter
Germany
From the indigo-coloured line in its spectrum.
Reich, who was colour-blind, was looking for thallium in sphalerite; his assistant Richter saw in its place a blue-indigo line never seen before.
It is obtained as a by-product of zinc, mostly in China and South Korea.
Touch screens and LCDs (indium tin oxide), solders, LEDs, solar panels.
Your phone screen is transparent and touch-sensitive thanks to indium. Bending a bar of indium makes it «cry».
Tin
Known since antiquity
From the Old English tin; the symbol Sn comes from the Latin stannum.
Mixed with copper it made bronze, which gave its name to the Bronze Age, over 5,000 years ago.
It is extracted from cassiterite (China, Indonesia, Myanmar, Peru).
Solder for electronics, tinplate for cans, bronze, float glass, organ pipes.
Bending a bar of tin makes a crackling sound called the «tin cry». Below 13 °C it can crumble into grey powder: the «tin pest».
Antimony
Known since antiquity
Of uncertain origin; the symbol Sb comes from stibium, the Latin name of stibnite.
Stibnite was used by the Egyptians as black eye make-up. The metal was described in detail in 1540 by Vannoccio Biringuccio of Siena.
It is extracted from stibnite, mostly in China, Russia and Tajikistan.
Flame retardants, lead-acid batteries, semiconductors, alloys for printing type.
Cleopatra lined her eyes with stibnite powder, a compound of antimony.
Tellurium
Franz-Joseph Müller von Reichenstein
Romania (Transylvania)
From the Latin tellus, «Earth».
Müller found it in 1782 in a gold ore from Transylvania. Klaproth confirmed the discovery and named it in 1798.
It is obtained from the sludge of copper refining.
Thin-film solar panels, rewritable discs, thermoelectric cells, alloys.
People who work with tellurium can have breath that smells of garlic for weeks!
Iodine
Bernard Courtois
France
From the Greek iodes, «violet», for the colour of its vapour.
Courtois was making saltpetre from seaweed for Napoleon's gunpowder; when he added acid, violet vapours rose up.
It is extracted from brines and from the nitrate deposits of Chile and from Japan; it is found in seaweed.
Disinfectants (tincture of iodine), iodised salt, contrast agents for X-rays, thyroid medicines.
The thyroid gland needs iodine: that is why iodised salt is sold.
Xenon
William Ramsay, Morris Travers
England
From the Greek xenos, «stranger».
It was the third gas found by Ramsay and Travers in liquid air in 1898. In 1962 Neil Bartlett made the first noble-gas compound, with xenon.
It is present in air in tiny traces (about 0.09 parts per million).
Xenon car headlights, flash lamps, ion thrusters for satellites, anaesthesia, cinema projector lamps.
The Dawn space probe and many satellites move through space with xenon ion engines.
Caesium
Robert Bunsen, Gustav Kirchhoff
Germany
From the Latin caesius, «sky blue», for the blue lines in its spectrum.
It was the first element discovered with the spectroscope, in 1860, by analysing the mineral water of Dürkheim: 40 tonnes of water were needed for a few grams of salt.
It is extracted from the mineral pollucite, mostly in Canada.
Atomic clocks, oil-drilling fluids, photoelectric cells.
The second is defined by the vibrations of caesium-133: exactly 9,192,631,770 oscillations.
Barium
Humphry Davy
England
From the Greek barys, «heavy».
Scheele recognised it in 1774; Davy isolated the metal in 1808 by electrolysis.
It is extracted from baryte (China, India, Morocco).
Drilling muds for oil wells, X-ray contrast agent (barium meal), green fireworks, glass.
The green in fireworks comes from barium.
Lanthanum
Carl Gustaf Mosander
Sweden
From the Greek lanthanein, «to lie hidden».
Mosander discovered it in 1839 hidden inside a cerium oxide: that is why he called it «the hidden one».
It is extracted from monazite and bastnäsite, mostly in China.
Camera lenses, batteries of hybrid cars (NiMH), catalysts for refining oil, lighters.
It gives its name to the whole lanthanide family, the «rare earths».
Cerium
Berzelius and Hisinger; Klaproth
Sweden / Germany
From the dwarf planet Ceres, discovered two years earlier (1801).
It was discovered in 1803 at the same time in Sweden and in Germany in the mineral cerite.
It is the most abundant rare earth; it is extracted from bastnäsite and monazite.
Lighter flints (ferrocerium), glass polishing, catalytic converters, self-cleaning ovens.
The sparks from lighter flints are tiny bits of cerium that catch fire when scraped.
Praseodymium
Carl Auer von Welsbach
Austria
From the Greek prasios didymos, «green twin».
«Didymium» was thought to be an element; in 1885 Auer von Welsbach split it into two: praseodymium (green salts) and neodymium.
It is extracted with the other rare earths from monazite and bastnäsite.
Powerful magnets, yellow glass, protective goggles for welders and glassblowers, aircraft engines.
The goggles of Murano glassblowers contain didymium, that is praseodymium and neodymium.
Neodymium
Carl Auer von Welsbach
Austria
From the Greek neos didymos, «new twin».
It was separated from «didymium» in 1885 together with praseodymium.
It is extracted mostly in China from bastnäsite and monazite.
The strongest magnets that exist: motors of electric cars, wind turbines, headphones, speakers, hard disks.
A small neodymium magnet can lift a thousand times its own weight.
